Release notes#

Status: final — tagged faber/v1.13.0 on 2026-10-12

Faber 1.13 turns the device route on: faber run can now execute @ kernel functions on the CPU and on Metal, with loops, reductions, run-time shapes and fault delivery, all in-process. Printed output finally follows the file's locale — an English program prints true / false / none, a Latin one true / false / none, on every backend. The raw-bits surface is settled (b8 b16 b32 b64, bytes as list<b8>), every type gains a written zero (Type {}), match matches several subjects at once, and reduction expressions lower across the main targets. The binary becomes self-contained: the standard library and the explain reference are embedded, and the separate host component is folded away. Several of these are breaking changes; read that section before you upgrade.

This is a consolidation release: its purpose is to capture the large body of language change that landed since 1.12 in one verifiable drop. It is good for writing, checking, formatting and interpreting Faber. It is not yet good for building real programs — compiled programs cannot yet touch the outside world, there is no way to install a library beyond the built-in standard library, and the standard library still has holes. Those limits are listed in detail under Known issues; none of them gate this release.

Language#

Output follows the file's locale. The words a program prints — boolean true / false (Latin true / false), the null value none (none), and the tuple head tuple (tuple) — come from the locale pack of the file that defines them, on every backend: the runner, Rust, Go, TypeScript, Swift, Python, WebAssembly, LLVM and the S-expression target. A generic function prints with the tokens of the unit that defines the template, not the caller. Haskell keeps its native True / False / Nothing. Expected-output files for corpus programs are written in the source's own locale. This closes the 1.12 defect where every locale printed the Latin words.

Raw bits and bytes. The bit-pattern markers b8, b16, b32 and b64 are the raw-bits domain: a bN is exactly N bits, always. ∧ ∨ ⊻ ¬ ⇐ ⇒ act at the type's width every time — a left shift drops bits off the top, a right shift fills with zeros, a shift by N or more gives all zeros, ¬ flips exactly N bits. A bN compares and orders by its unsigned bit pattern and does no arithmetic. Conversions are explicit ↦: same-width bN to iN is two's complement, bN to f16 / bf16 / f32 / f64 reinterprets the bit pattern (both ways), and a byte list and a wider-element list convert through each other with via Le or via Be for little- or big-endian packing. The old escape hatches are gone: `via Bits no longer converts through a bits view, the words byte / octeti` are retired (list<b8> is the byte list), and ≠ is retired in favour of ≢ as the negation of ≡. A bit-type value or a list window that a target has no carrier for is refused by name at emit time, not approximated.

The zero of a type is written `Type {}`. tensor<T, [shape]> {}, vector<T, N> {}, matrix<T, [r, c]> {} and the short sugar tf32[2, 2] {} build the typed zero: every part takes its default, including a tensor of vectors and size-parameter extents. The bare form (← tf32[2, 2]) is retired, as is Type []; a call-form constructor is refused at parse time. The inferred constructor _ {} builds the typed zero where the type comes from context. empty (Latin empty) is the default empty instance of the declared type: at a dense tensor, vector or matrix slot it is the typed zero. empty claims zero-or-more types only — a text, character, byte, regex or tuple slot refuses it by name. The English reader spells the marker empty now; the earlier English spelling empty is gone.

Multi-subject `match`. match a and b matches several subjects at once, with one pattern per arm over all subjects. The match is over closed sets: every arm's pattern is checked for exhaustiveness against the subjects' constructors, width and length-shape patterns are rejected, and a match over a value-type subject is refused by name with a hint to switch forms. It lowers on the MIR runner as a tag-probe chain and emits on Go and TypeScript as a column-probe chain and on Swift as a tuple pattern per arm.

Reduction expressions. The reduce reduction family is in the language and lowered on the runner, Rust, Go and TypeScript: plain reductions fold to a flat walk, grouped reductions (with per) and the argument-extrema forms (argmax / argmin) lower, an optional reduction is a native option value, and a reduction body with statements runs in a value closure. The for statement accepts a thread clause, so a loop can carry a thread argument through its body. A failable read inside a kernel's lane body may take an inline default.

Conversion rounding is explicit. A conversion from a float or a decimal to an integer, inf or a policy-word cell now names its rounding: via Floor, via Ceil, via HalfEven or via Trunc (half-even is the default everywhere else). A bare float-to-integer conversion is rejected by name; write the hint. Convert-assign accepts the hint too (`a ↤ x via Trunc ⊥ 0`), keeping the failable error path. The runner, the S-expression, WebAssembly and the Rust, TypeScript, Go, Swift and Python emitters honour the four modes.

Checked tensor access. The method forms accipe (get) and ponde (set) are the failable tensor reads and writes: out-of-range fails through the ordinary error channel, on the runner, on generated Rust, TypeScript and Go, and on the device route inside kernels. The bracket forms stay plain T and trap on a bad index, and a literal index provably out of bounds stays a compile error. A checked store is failable unless its index is proven in range.

Aggregates: arithmetic, aliases and ownership. Arithmetic over lists, queues and stacks follows one rule set: ⊙ and ⊘ (and ÷, % and unary minus where they apply) operate element-wise over two aggregates, and the bounded-list length defects are fixed. An alias of an unmarked list, map, object, queue or contract parameter is read-only, exactly like the parameter itself, and the bind-alias rule is flow-aware: an unconditional re-bind of the source detaches its stale aliases. Conversely, own and copy parameters are writable by the callee — field stores, element stores, reassignment and mutating methods all work on them — and mutation of a read-only binding is counted by a warning. A device launch whose written binding overlaps another binding is refused up front (the noalias contract).

Smaller settled rules.

  • The right-hand side of is is always a type; the null words split from the null type. A bare none value is a named parse error that names the locale's word (null in English, null in Latin); none survives only as the Latin null type and in case none patterns.
  • An optional stored into a plain cell — at an argument, return, field initializer, throw, yield, element or tuple store — is rejected by name; unwrap or convert first.
  • Flow narrowing works through and, or and not conditions, and a diverging or-guard ends the path.
  • The keyed list method .sorted(key) (Latin .ordinata(key)) is retired in favour of the sort expression; the standard library's ordered_map module is renamed sorted_map (the Latin word is unchanged).
  • A text index s[i] yields the Unicode character everywhere, including generated Rust; the optional text read get / accipe returns the character or none past the end on Rust, Go, TypeScript and Swift.
  • The mean of an empty tensor is NaN (sum over count) on every runtime; the grammar records the sentence.
  • Trailing commas in array element lists are a parse error.
  • JSON parsing reads integer tokens of any length into the unbounded integer type; JSON documents parse and serialize in pure Faber, including object-rooted documents.
  • cumulate folds into a fresh accumulator (the caller's value is no longer overwritten); int ↦ f32 rounds once on Python; a map holding an enum or variant value prints like the runner on the S-expression target; list and map values convert to and from the dynamic value element-wise on Rust, and the LLVM conversion no longer fails.

Tooling#

A self-contained binary. The standard library (Norma) is embedded in the faber binary the way the runtime sources already were, and the explain reference is embedded too. The library home no longer probes a build checkout: an installed faber resolves the standard library with no environment variables set, and the release smoke proves it. The native host surface — file, network, HTTP, console — lives in this repository now; the release manifest pins this repository alone, with no separate host component.

`faber corpus`. A new product command verifies target code end to end. It runs a named suite of exemplar cases through one target per invocation (--target rust, --target runner, …), where each case pins its expected outcome — pass, expected-fail, or not applicable — in a checked-in expectation file. The command validates what each target can judge, bounds every child process, and never hides a pass behind a skipped phase; a failing case is either a regression or a stale expectation. Suites cover the exempla corpus, the product packages and the GPU rungs.

`faber format`. Formatting policy is configurable: a [format] section in the package manifest sets the policy (and the CLI value wins over the manifest, which wins over the built-in default normalise-v1; the pretty-v1 style is admitted with a rebaselined corpus). The steady-state flags are --write (in place), --stdin / --stdout (one document through the pipe; --stdout takes exactly one input file), and --policy <slug> (unknown slugs fail clearly). --canonical is gone — --locale is the only re-emit selector — and asking for both a policy and a locale re-emission is rejected explicitly rather than silently switching modes.

Installer lifecycle. The bootstrap installer is verified end to end. faber self update fetches the installer base, faber self repair runs a typed repair policy, faber self uninstall removes only what the product owns, and a downgrade to an incompatible pack fails closed instead of mixing. Reinstall is idempotent. An HTTPS-to-HTTP redirect on installer or HTTP fetch is refused.

Locale flags. --locale (formerly --reader-locale) selects the source locale, and the new --diagnostics-locale selects the language of diagnostics independently of it. Diagnostics carry the locale id and issue name, and parse errors print the locale pack's own keyword spelling.

Generated code. Generated output prints the display tokens of the module it was compiled from, so English source prints true / false / none on every target. Every failable function in generated Swift is a throws function (the result-wrapper path is gone), so regenerate Swift output. Go carries a class as a pointer with a zero value and &T{} constructors, removing the interface-pointer workarounds. Unreachable markers and expect calls are gone from the TypeScript, Go, Swift, Python and WebAssembly emitters. A new default-off novelty target joins the experimental set: Odin (faber emit -t odin), a fail-closed scalar-and-print subset behind the hir-odin feature, listed by faber targets as unavailable on a default build.

GPU#

faber run --device … executes device code for real.

  • --device cpu runs @ kernel functions on the MIR runner in host form — device programs are testable without a GPU.
  • --device metal runs them on Metal through an in-process device session; the child-process route is retired. The device route serves --stats, program arguments and every input kind, and its output matches the CPU route.
  • --device auto prepares the package once and reuses the lowered unit.
  • faber test --device cpu runs a package's kernel rows in host form; the auto, metal and cuda selections refuse with a clear exit for now. Run and test share one device-selection precedence.

Kernel launches support lane-form bodies with loops, break, continue and early return; run-time extents flow through the dispatcher, so a kernel can take N-dimensional tensor indices and shapes decided at launch; a class parameter rides along as a packed parameter block read on the GPU; and vector-element tensors (width 2 and 4) upload and read back. Whole-grid reductions run on the device, and matmul accepts run-time dimensions on Metal, verified against the CPU oracle across the tiled, one-row, gemv and simdgroup shapes. Every buffer binding is 16-byte aligned and refused before encoding if it is not.

Faults are part of the contract: a kernel declaring an error channel can throw a constant text, an unproven index guards with an unsigned compare and a lowest-lane-wins fault word, and the fault is delivered to the enclosing do all or plain do on the real Metal route. do all … while is legal grammar, and a host read after a faulting launch delivers the fault before the read completes.

Breaking changes#

  1. `≠` is retired. Write ≢ for the negation of ≡; ≠ draws the named parse error that names its replacement.
  2. `via Bits` is retired. Convert through the bit markers: x ↦ b32, u16 ↦ b16 ↦ f16, and the bN conversion table above.
  3. `byte` / `octeti` are retired. Bytes are list<b8>; the byte literal and byte insertion produce a list<b8> everywhere.
  4. A bare float-to-integer conversion is rejected. Name the rounding: via Floor, via Ceil, via HalfEven or via Trunc (the error names them).
  5. The typed zero is `Type {}`. Rewrite the bare form ← tf32[2, 2] as tf32[2, 2] {}; Type [] and call-form constructors are refused.
  6. A bare `none` value is retired. Write null (Latin null); the parse error names the locale's word.
  7. English `empty` is retired. The English empty-instance marker is empty; Latin keeps empty.
  8. `.sorted(key)` is retired in favour of the sort expression, and the ordered_map module is renamed sorted_map.
  9. CLI renames. --reader-locale is --locale; diagnostics move to the new --diagnostics-locale; faber format --canonical is gone (--locale is the only re-emit selector).
  10. The file-copy verbs in the native host surface are renamed: copy / copy_async are exscribe / exscribet.
  11. Regenerate generated code. Swift output from 1.12 does not match the new throws emission, and Go class output changed shape. Older output and this release's runtimes do not mix.
  12. Trailing commas in array element lists are a parse error.

Known issues#

The three limits below shape what 1.13 is for. It is for people who want to read, write and check the language as it now stands, and run scripts through the interpreter. Anyone who wants to ship a compiled program that reads a file, or use the graphics, autograd or UI libraries, should wait for the releases that close those limits.

  • A built program cannot touch the outside world. faber build --target rust works for pure code — math, text, print. The moment a program uses the file-system, console, process or random modules, the build stops with PKG001 package_host_selection_required, and host = "native" answers host_provider_unsupported: the native host provider was retired on purpose and its replacement has not landed. Interpreted runs keep script I/O — faber run covers file read and write, console, the current directory, environment variables and random.
  • There is no way to add a library. The graphics, autograd and UI libraries cannot be installed; faber doctor reports all three not-found. Only the built-in standard library ships with the binary, and the package manager is not released yet, so there is no install command.
  • The standard library has holes. time.now() fails under faber run; there is no working HTTP route and no WebSocket surface; and roughly seventy standard-library lines are marked deferred — functions that exist by name and fail when called, with text, encoding, toml and net among them.
  • Some shipped exemplars are stale. One imports norma:solum, a module name that no longer exists; three exemplar packages fail faber check, and that failure reports a line far beyond the end of the file, so the diagnostic points at the wrong place.

Beyond those limits:

  • The largest device acceptance case cannot meet its bound as written. The full-grid flood simulation (roughly 1,227 by 1,132 cells) completes on Metal, but its f32 depth field differs from the reference by more than the 0.01 m bound allows — the bound presumes arithmetic bit-identical to the donor program, and a one-ulp change of one input cell moves the field by metres between runs. The reduced-grid oracle passes on Metal within the bound.
  • A throwing kernel can throw only a constant text, and kernel-to-kernel inlining of a throwing kernel is not implemented.
  • Regex engine gaps by target (carried from 1.12): Go has no Unicode \b; TypeScript clears repeated-group captures per iteration; Swift and Python differ from the dialect on named constructs; the backtracking engines (TypeScript, Python, Swift) can take exponential time on hostile patterns; Racket and Haskell name every regex construct unsupported.
  • Range containment `∈ a‥b` still has no MIR lowering; it emits on the HIR targets only.
  • Rust corpus builds. One corpus program still fails to build on Rust (it stores an awaited promise at a ← binding); it is recorded as an expected failure. The half-width float cells (f16, bf16 and their policy words) build again on Rust; bare f16 / bf16 ride an f32 carrier.
  • Print and templates (carried): the comma form print a, b still lays out differently on the MIR text targets than elsewhere; LLVM still lacks template rows for some sized integers and composites; Haskell still rejects string templates. Prefer a template, print "§ §"(a, b).
  • `faber convert` still does not resolve imports; a file importing a library type fails with the resolution error.
  • Checker residuals (carried): narrowing an inferred error result with is and ✓ ✗ is still accepted by the checker and rejected only at MIR validation; WebAssembly still types one conversion local as f64; the Go, Python and Swift generic-enum and generic-map gaps remain.
  • Device-row test debt. A sizable slice of the kernel test rows for the autograd library fails under faber test --device cpu on empty-initialised tensors — a library-side initialization issue, not a launch refusal.
  • Experimental targets differ from `faber run` where their arithmetic does (carried): COBOL checks only stored values, Pascal traps per operation, BASIC floats are the C64's. Each target rejects the cases it cannot match by name.
  • Sibling-library gates. No gate in this repository runs the autograd or UI libraries' suites; the optional graphics provider package checks and the environment-gated device checks remain skipped (carried from 1.10).

Not in this release#

  • Character ranges as set bounds (x ∈ '0'…'9') are still not supported; interval bounds are numbers, and text membership stays .contains.
  • The slash regex literal and per-group spans are not shipped; read group spans with start() and group(n).
  • The collection-ergonomics rewrite, set-algebra glyphs and superscript powers remain planned.
  • Removal of the comma print form is still decided in direction only.
  • externa typing and conditional-compilation enforcement stay held; there is no LSP.
  • Translated reader packs keep their own spelling for the null type until the word is chosen.
  • Public publication of the Go runtime module and @faber/runtime waits for the Faber 2 migration; they are consumed by path here.
  • The CUDA backend exists behind hardware-gated checks; no CUDA route is enabled for faber run.
  • The Lean leaf is not a discoverable target or package backend.
  • Radix stays at 0.84.0 (no separate Radix release); Cista is unchanged and not part of this release.
